text: A loop between tickets is almost never a real two-way need: read both plan tasks and classify (wrong direction, verify-only, false claim, split, step in wrong ticket). Run a cycle and self-link check on every new link set before solving.
why: Of 17 + 13 loops read, 0 were real two-way; 13 of 44 new links formed loops and 9 were self-links.

text: Greedy scheduling gives an upper bound only. Use the exact CP-SAT model and compute a lower bound (total SP over total capacity) before reporting an end sprint.
why: A greedy run showed Sprint 17 for a plan the solver ends in Sprint 14; adding capacity made the greedy result worse.

text: Optimize in two steps: first the end sprint, then owner changes or the owner's load preference. A hard minimum per person can make the solver find nothing; use a soft shortfall term seeded with a nearby plan.
why: Hard 240 SP minimums returned UNKNOWN; the soft version found a valid plan.

text: Verify a schedule with a different code path than the one that built it, and state what was excluded. Add a file-ordering check (a file a ticket modifies must be created earlier) before saying nobody is blocked.
why: A scheduler regex dropped an edge; a file-level check found 13 orderings the link-level checks missed.

text: Say the covered fraction every time. Two agreeing readers show consistency, not correctness; sample controls (about 60 clean-looking tickets) and use an adversarial auditor told to refute.
why: A control sample of 60 clean-looking tickets had 6 not clean after two readers said READY.

text: Answer the question first. Report counts, not ticket keys, in chat; never print git author fields or emails. When naming a wait, arm a monitor and check at that time.

text: For more than about 30 agents use a workflow, not hand-launched waves. Units of 5 tickets, depth gate by script (at least 4 real needs checked, resolution at least 200 characters), then a second agent told to refute every non-READY verdict and caveat.

text: To redo a few failed units, launch a new run on only those units. Do not resume: the resume cache stops at the first failed call and reruns every call after it (about 150 finished units reran, about 10 million tokens).
why: A resume meant for 6 units reran 150.

text: Tell every agent: read-only, one output file, no helper files (not even /tmp), no env vars or emails. Cap tool calls and require UNSURE instead of READY on any assumption.

text: Run one long ticket through any bulk pipeline and check output limits before a bulk run.

text: Replan incrementally: run plan-store stale (plan task text, Jira updated stamp, code files and producers fingerprinted per verdict) and send only stale tickets to agents. Tickets now Done leave the plan. Cycle-check new links, re-solve with warm start, check, export. See docs/jira/REPLAN.md.

text: Promote a mention in audit evidence to an enforced link only after a targeted check. After verifying the 46 that the plan violated, 1 was real and 5 more pointed at the right sibling part.
why: Loose links over-constrain; verifying only the violated ones cost about 0.4M tokens.

text: Solve in two stages: first fix each ticket's owner as in the last valid plan and solve only the sprints (small exact problem; INFEASIBLE there is a proof the owners must change), then free the owners and polish. Always validate the output against the real set of people: a config key such as default is a capacity, never a person.
why: A blind full-model repair returned UNKNOWN for 7 minutes; the owners-fixed stage solved optimally in 59 seconds. A solver treated the config key default as a fifth person and gave one real person 0 SP.

text: Record every producer an audit relied on as a link in the graph, not only the blocks. Audits judged against one schedule while the final schedule moved 915 of 1,397 tickets; links make later schedules respect what the audit verified.
why: Only blocks were enforced, so cleared needs could be broken by a later schedule.
